description: Alpha and Omega Semiconductor Limited designs, develops, and supplies power semiconductor products for computing, consumer electronics, communication, and industrial applications in Hong Kong, China,
description_full: Alpha and Omega Semiconductor Limited designs, develops, and supplies power semiconductor products for computing, consumer electronics, communication, and industrial applications in Hong Kong, China, South Korea, the United States, and internationally. The company offers power discrete products, including industry standard trench metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs), Shielded-Gate low- and mid-voltage MOSFETs, SuperJunction high-voltage MOSFETs, and trench-stop insulated gate bipolar transistors, as well as application-specific MOSFETs for smartphone battery management, dual MOSFETs for CPU power conversion, and high-power density MOSFETs for IBC power modules in AI data centers. It also provides power IC products, total power solutions for Intel panther lake and wildcat lake platforms, and the SmartClamp family of protected DrMOS for AI servers, data centers, and high-end graphics cards, as well as silicon carbide, IPM, HV gate drivers, and digital power products. Alpha and Omega Semiconductor Limited was incorporated in 2000 and is headquartered in Sunnyvale, California.

financial_summary: Alpha and Omega Semiconductor L is a small-cap technology business with a $716M market cap on $679M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at -1% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The company is burning through $68M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin -55.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 17% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
